title: Find a Value in a Sorted Grid
statement:
You get a grid grid with rows rows and cols columns. It is sorted like a page of text read left to right, top to bottom:

  • each row is sorted ascending, and
  • the first value of each row is larger than the last value of the row above it.

Return true if target appears in the grid, otherwise false. Your solution must run in O(log(rows · cols)) time.

examples.why: 15 is in the middle row. Reading the grid row by row gives one sorted list of 9 values, and 15 is at position 5.
8 falls in the gap between the end of row 0 (7) and the start of row 1 (10). A row search that picks "the row whose first value is ≤ 8" picks row 0 and must still say no.
The grid is not square. Turning position 6 into a cell needs row = 6 / cols and col = 6 % cols; dividing by rows instead lands on the wrong cell.

constraints: Read row by row, the values are strictly increasing
hints: If you wrote all the rows one after another, what would that long list look like?
You do not need to build that list. Given a position p in it, which row and which column does it live in?
Binary search over positions 0 … rows·cols − 1, reading cell (floor(p / cols), p % cols). Or binary search the first column to pick a row, then search inside that row.

explain.intuition:
The two rules mean the grid is really one sorted list that has been wrapped onto several lines, like a paragraph in a fixed-width box. So you can run an ordinary binary search over positions 0 … rows·cols − 1 and only translate a position into a cell when you need to read it: row = floor(p / cols), col = p % cols.

The other common route is two searches: first find the last row whose first value is ≤ target, then search inside that row. It is the same O(log rows + log cols), but it has two places to get an edge wrong instead of one.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = rows · cols − 1, an inclusive range of positions.
While lo <= hi, take mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2) and read v = grid[floor(mid / cols)][mid % cols].
If v < target set lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid − 1.
pitfalls: Dividing by rows instead of cols when turning a position into a cell. It works on square grids and breaks on every other shape.
In the two-search version, picking the row with grid[mid][0] < target instead of <=. When target is the first value of a row, you then search the row above and miss it.
Starting with hi = rows · cols in an inclusive search. The first mid can then point one past the last cell and read off the end of the grid.

solutions.title: Check every cell
solutions.idea: Scan the whole grid. O(rows · cols), ignores the order.

solutions.title: Pick the row, then search it
solutions.idea: Binary search the first column for the last row that starts at or below target. Only that row can hold target; binary search inside it.

solutions.title: One search over the unrolled grid
solutions.idea: Treat the grid as one sorted list of rows · cols values and translate each probed position into (row, col).

followups: Each row and each column is sorted, but rows no longer continue from the row above. Binary search no longer works directly; what does? (Hint: start at the top-right corner.)
The grid is stored as one flat array of length rows · cols, the way image pixels usually are. What changes in the code, and what stays the same?
